report:
Conclusion: The claim is not supported; current evidence points away from influenza vaccination causing Alzheimer’s disease. Large observational studies and reviews generally report no increased risk—and often a lower dementia/Alzheimer’s risk among vaccinated older adults—though this does not prove vaccination prevents Alzheimer’s because of healthy-vaccinee bias and residual confounding.

A propensity-matched U.S. claims cohort of adults ≥65 found influenza vaccination was associated with reduced Alzheimer’s risk over follow-up: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9484126/. A 2022 systematic review/meta-analysis concluded influenza vaccination was associated with significantly lower dementia risk: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1568163721002816. A later review noted evidence can be inconsistent by subgroup and study design, but still evaluated risk reduction rather than harm: https://academic.oup.com/ageing/article/54/7/afaf169/8182144. A broader 2025 systematic review reported adult vaccinations, including influenza, were associated with lower dementia risk: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41269248/.

Bottom line: there is no credible evidence that flu vaccination causes Alzheimer’s disease; the balance of evidence suggests neutral-to-protective associations, while causality for prevention remains unproven.
